title: TB9-31372
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of China who appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated October 28, 2019, rejecting his refugee claim.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of China who appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated October 28, 2019, rejecting his refugee claim. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration Canada had intervened based on the issue of credibility and was present at the Appellant's hearing.

The Appellant argues that the RPD was wrong to find that his account lacked credibility. After conducting an independent analysis, I find that the RPD was correct to find that he lacked credibility. The appeal is therefore dismissed.

The Appellant alleges that he is being sought by the Public Security Bureau (PSB) in China because of his religious beliefs. He discovered the Local Church of China, also known as the Shouters, after he had developed a gambling problem and subsequently become depressed and suicidal.
His aunt introduced him to the above Christian sect in XXXX 2016 and he was persuaded initially to pray at home and later to attend house church services.

On XXXX XXXX, 2017 the church was raided and the Appellant along with two others were arrested and interrogated because of their religious activities. After two days in detention, he was required to pay a fine of XXXX XXXX before release and given conditions to report whenever summoned. Following this incident, the Appellant and his family sought the assistance of a smuggler to help him depart from China. He arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017 and learned that the PSB had summoned him for investigation on XXXX XXXX, 2017. Thus, he filed his refugee claim shortly thereafter.

The standard of review is correctness as established in Huruglica1, where the Federal Court of Appeal gives guidance in regard to the role of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). ANALYSIS Memorandum of Appeal
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: The determinative issue on appeal is credibility. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of his credibility; i) by making a negative inference from his failure to disclose previous refugee applications and using this and other inconsistencies between his applications to impugn all of his credibility, ii) by determining that his documentary evidence and testimony were not credible based on inconsistencies regarding his family and personal background which were peripheral issues and by dismissing documents regarding the same based solely on the availability of fraudulent documents, iii) by determining that previous misrepresentation about his wife's name meant that the part she played in his narrative was false, iv) by either failing to analyse documents supplied in support of the claim or dismissing some without due consideration, v) by failing to apply the proper legal test in determining sur place and focusing on motivation rather than merits of the documents and by finding that activities in China were relevant to a sur place analysis.

The Appellant is not relying on any new evidence referred to in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and does not request an oral hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA. Findings related to Credibility Failure to disclose time and applications made in Australia
I find that the RPD was correct regarding its overall finding about the impact of the Appellant's failure to disclose his time in Australia on his refugee claim in Canada.

The RPD found that the Appellant did not reasonably explain his failure to disclose his Australian residence or the inconsistencies between the information he provided to Australian authorities versus Canadian authorities, particularly about his wife's name and date of birth; as well as his father's date of death, his work and his address. The RPD found that overall the Appellant's actions conveyed a deliberate attempt to conceal his personal travel history and as such the Appellant had lost the benefit of the presumption of truthfulness.

The Appellant argues that it was an error to draw a negative credibility inference from his failure to disclose his previous refugee applications in Australia, given the failure to disclose was attributable to duress. He submits that his failure to disclose this information and inconsistencies between the Australian and Canadian refugee applications were used to determine he was not credible regarding his religious belief. However, he was entitled to the presumption of truth and plausibility findings can only be made in the clearest of cases. He submits that his failure to disclose was insufficient to deny him the presumption of truthfulness or to find that his credibility was undermined in its entirety. He argues that he was dependent upon the smuggler to facilitate his entry and he had to obey the smugglers instructions given his passport had been confiscated. He argues that he was prevented from pursuing other options and the smuggler's actions coerced him into obedience because the smuggler had power over him, so the RPD mischaracterized the situation by indicating that he relied upon the smuggler's advice.

I have reviewed the Appellant's testimony in this regard. At the hearing he testified that he was in Australia from 2009 until 2016 and made two applications for refugee protection during that time on the basis of political problems he experienced in China. He testified that he did not declare to Canadian authorities that he had made a refugee claim in Australia because the smuggler repeatedly told him not to disclose this information to Canadian authorities as he would have problems obtaining protection in Canada if he did.

He also testified about the things the smuggler did for him when describing how he managed to leave China. He explained that the smuggler/snakehead assisted him with getting a Canadian temporary resident visa, had someone pick him up after he arrived in Canada, arranged for his accommodations, and accompanied him to Canada. For this he paid XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

I find that the failure to disclose these applications was a significant omission. While the Appellant suggests that he was under duress, I do not find this to be the case nor do I find that the RPD mischaracterized the situation. The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017 and made his claim for refugee protection inland at CIC Etobicoke a few weeks later on XXXX XXXX, 2017. He did not make his claim upon entry in the presence of the smuggler. Further, there is also no indication in the evidence that the smuggler threatened to withhold his passport on the basis of his disclosure/non-disclosure of the information about the Australian claims. The smuggler simply told him that providing such information may have a certain consequence (on the claim), but not one imposed by the smuggler.

According to the Appellant's evidence, while the smuggler gave him information or advice, the Appellant was not forced to comply, nor was he under duress as suggested in the memorandum. He chose to follow said advice because he trusted this individual who saw him out of China safely.

It is anticipated that persons will be forthcoming with Canadian authorities from whom they are seeking assistance and I find that this was a significant omission, which does seriously undermine the credibility of his entire account given that the information about his residence in Australia only came to light as a result of the Minister's intervention in the case.

While he submits that he is entitled to the presumption of truthfulness, I find that this presumption only applies when there is no reason to doubt the testimony. However, given the credibility concerns that exist based on the fact that the Appellant concealed that he resided in Australia for several years and presented entirely different reasons for fearing persecution as well as different basic details about his family and work history without a reasonable explanation, I find that this does undermine the credibility of his overall account.

He in fact had no explanation for why his wife's name and date of birth were recorded differently by Australian authorities, nor did he have an explanation for why his father's date of death was recorded incorrectly in his Basis of Claim form. Given his wife's close relationship to him as well as the circumstances surrounding his father's death and the significant events that followed (to be discussed below), I find also that it is not reasonable that these details were inconsistent.
I have conducted an independent assessment and I find that the Appellant lacks credibility. Omission of political profile

I find that there is also an additional omission regarding the Appellant's imputed political opinion that is relevant and illustrates his lack of credibility. I have considered the caselaw on what constitutes a new issue. As per Corvil2, a recent Federal court case: It goes without saying that when considering a question which was not raised before the RPD or by any of the parties to the appeal, the RAD must first notify the parties accordingly and give them an opportunity to respond thereto (Ching v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 725 at para 71 [Ching]). However, it is now a well-established fact that when the credibility of a refugee protection claimant is at the heart of the RPD's decision and the grounds for appeal before the RAD, the RAD is entitled to make independent findings in this regard, without having to question the applicant or giving the applicant another opportunity to make submissions. That said, the RAD must avoid disregarding contradictory evidence on the record or making findings based on evidence unknown to the applicant (Ibrahim v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 380 at paras 26, 30 [Ibrahim]; Koffi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 4 at para 38; Kwakwa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 600 at para 24; Marin v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 243 at paras 35-37 [Rodriguez Marin]; Oluwaseyi Adeoye v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 246 at para 13 [Adeoye]). In this case, credibility was at the heart of the RPD's concerns and the subsequent rejection of the applicant's claim for refugee protection. It was also at the heart of the applicant's appeal to the RAD. Therefore, the RAD's independent finding regarding the date of issue of the Canadian visa affecting the applicant's credibility did not constitute a new issue, in and of itself, and did not involve contradictory evidence. Was this finding based on evidence unknown to the applicant? The answer is no, since the date of issue of the Canadian visa is clearly indicated in the record (Certified Tribunal Record [CTR] at pp 76, 102).

Given the above caselaw, I find that this omission cannot be considered a new issue. I do not find that the Appellant would be taken by surprise because this omission was raised at the RPD hearing and the Appellant had a full opportunity to answer to the concerns. Credibility is the central issue in both the RPD decision and on appeal. Further, the omission is very closely related to the issues raised on appeal, in particular the points above regarding his failure to disclose his unsuccessful Australian refugee applications and this omission further illustrates the problems in this claim. As this is not a new issue, I am not required to provide notice to the Appellant and give him a further opportunity to respond.

The Appellant confirmed in testimony that the information he had provided to Australian authorities was true, complete and correct. He verified that his father and brother were involved in a serious accident in XXXX 2005 and his father died later in hospital as a result of the serious injuries sustained. He verified that some drunken XXXX XXXX XXXX were responsible. His brother was subsequently arrested for inciting anti-government activities and was sentenced to reform through labour for three years in XXXX 2005. When asked why he did not include these details, which were the basis of his claim in Australia in his Canadian Basis of Claim (BOC) form, he indicated again that the smuggler told him not to mention anything that he told Australian authorities. He then confirmed that his elder brother was also arrested in 2008 and sentenced to labour education camp for three years and that from XXXX 2008 until XXXX 2009 he (the Appellant) had organized ten people to distribute copies of pamphlets. He testified that he decided to leave China after that because the Chinese government wanted to arrest him based on what happened with his father's death and accident as well as because he had been distributing flyers. When asked again why he did not include these details in his Canadian BOC he testified that the smuggler told him not to reveal anything that he had reported to the Australian government.

When he returned to China, he testified that he did not have any difficulty with the PSB because he did not return to his own home, but rather he stayed with friends in a different province. He expanded on this when the member asked about how he managed to avoid detention or arrest given his previous political activity. He explained that it was the local police officers/ the Fuqing PSB that were after him, but the airport he arrived at was in Fuzhou so he did not have problems other than being taken into a room and asked to register, which was not a common occurrence.

He also indicated in his testimony that he sought the assistance of an agent to help him to apply for a new passport because he dared not go by himself, given the incident that had occurred with his father and older brother and that the PSB would want him as indicated in the summons he had received. Later, when asked why he was making a refugee claim in Canada, the Appellant testified it was because his church was raided, he had been detained and fined so he was terrified. He also testified, "On top, after I came back from Australia that incident that happened to father and brother I never received final notice from the government. All those combined I thought I had to leave China."

I find that particularly given that the political problems with the local Fuqing PSB are apparently unresolved/ongoing and according to his own testimony, this formed part of the reason that he came to Canada, at the very least he should have included these details in his BOC narrative in Canada. His explanation, that the smuggler told him not to say anything, is not persuasive. Withholding the fact that he had made a claim elsewhere is one thing, but I find it is also not reasonable that he did not mention these details about the problems he was facing as a result of his family and his own political activities given they form part of his reasons for departing from China and fearing return.

According to the Australian claims for protection,3 one brother unsuccessfully sued the XXXX who never took responsibility for killing their father. His eldest brother was accused of inciting workers to strike and disturbing normal social orders after trying, again unsuccessfully, to secure compensation for his wife who had been paralyzed in a serious accident at work. After these incidents the Appellant himself, after becoming disillusioned with the government, organized others to hand out anti-government pamphlets - which brought him to the attention of police who went to his home in XXXX 2009 and interrogated his wife. These are not minor or unrelated past incidents as put forward at the hearing. He signed his BOC to indicate that the information he provided was true, complete and correct and this information is not found in his narrative. I find that this was a significant omission and it is not credible that he would not include all the reasons that he is being sought/faces a risk in China. I find that this further undermines the overall credibility of his allegations. Summons

The RPD found that the summons was not a credible or reliable document because it did not believe the underlying facts upon which the summons was created. It disbelieved that the Appellant was a genuine Christian Shouter and therefore that the Appellant was wanted by the Chinese authorities.

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred by failing to analyze the evidence provided in support of the claim, for example the marriage certificate, business license, outpatient record and photos. They argue that even where it did consider certain items; namely the summons, that it was dismissed without due consideration.
I agree that the summons was not assessed separately. As such, I will conduct my own independent assessment of the document below.

I have closely examined the summons4 that was before the RPD and was tendered to show that the principal Appellant was wanted by the Chinese authorities. When compared to the available samples, the Chinese characters found at the top of the summons on the second line, which identify the summons type, match the sample for the public security summons (zhi'an chuanhuan). Thus, I compared the document to the sample.

According to the National Documentation Package (NDP), summonses have not varied in format since 2003. Further, the same document indicates that "...such forms are supposed to be used throughout the country and that regional variations are not meant to exist." Hence, the summons in evidence should duplicate the sample in terms of its format and structure.

However, I find that the summons in evidence differs from the sample5 contained within the NDP. Firstly, four lines down, on the left side of the document, the sample has one word/character, followed by a colon, whereas the summons proffered by the Appellant has three Chinese characters preceding the colon, none of which match the Chinese character on the sample. In reviewing the English translation6 of the sample, it reveals that the missing Chinese character corresponds with the salutation addressing the person concerned; To: which is meant to be standard text and is not found on the summons in evidence.

In the main body of the document (the three lines that follow), the second and third lines of the summons in evidence do not match the sample. The first Chinese character on the second line is missing from the summons in evidence; there are six Chinese characters which precede the >> symbol on the sample, whereas in the summons in evidence there are only five Chinese characters in the same spot. Similarly, the Chinese characters preceding the reporting date (which are not underlined) do not match. The summons in evidence has five Chinese characters where the sample has only three. The third line is also at odds as the number 22, the Chinese character that follows it and the number 10 that appear on the third line of the summons in evidence should fall on the second rather than the third line according to the sample.

In addition, there is a fourth line of centred text on the summons in evidence that does not appear in the sample at all. Further midway down the page, a stamp appears over two lines of text. In the first line of that text there are only five Chinese characters within the set of brackets, whereas in the sample there are six Chinese characters within the brackets in the same spot. Furthermore, on the line that follows where the date is written in English as 2017/XXXX XXXX XXXX on the summons in evidence, in the sample that information appears entirely in Chinese characters.
Finally, in the bottom three lines of text, the Chinese character at the beginning of the second line differs from the Chinese character in the sample that appears at the same spot.

In Jiang7, Justice Crampton found that small differences can be telling: In my view, it may very well be reasonably open to the RAD or another decision maker to question the authenticity of a document based on very small or even microscopic differences between the document and an authentic counterpart. It is in the small or microscopic details where a forgery may well be exposed.

I find on a balance of probabilities, that the summons submitted is fraudulent, and that the Appellant's submission of a fraudulent document in support of his case significantly undermines his credibility.

This summons was specifically provided to illustrate that the Appellant is wanted by the Chinese authorities for being part of a dangerous illegal church. Given my finding that the summons is fraudulent, I also find on a balance of probabilities that the Appellant is not being investigated nor is he wanted by the PSB for being a member of the Christian Shouter church as alleged.

The only other document which deals directly with his issues with the PSB because of his participation in the Christian Shouters group in China is a receipt for a fine he allegedly paid as a result of preaching a "dangerous illegal religion and damaging the social order."8 The RPD did not expressly refer to this particular document in its decision, therefore I will as part of my independent assessment.

I note that as per case law, submitting a false or irregular document may have an impact on the weight assigned to other documents provided by the Appellant, especially when they are interrelated,9 and on the overall credibility of an Appellant.10 I find that given the use of a fraudulent summons, that no weight can be put on this letter, which was allegedly issued in relation to the same event and by the same entity; the Fuqing city PSB.

While it is true that he possessed some knowledge of the faith, the Appellant has alleged that he had been attending a church since his arrival in Canada. As such, the knowledge he has could easily have been gained in Canada. I note that simply having some information regarding basic teachings and practice or the lack of such information does not necessarily reflect genuine or false practice. I find that little weight can be given to the Appellant's ability to answer questions about Shouter Christians and his correct responses do not overcome the serious credibility concerns in this case.

I find that given the serious credibility findings as outlined above; his failure to disclose his time and two previous applications for refugee protection made in Australia, the significant omission of one of the reasons why he seeks protection in Canada, and the submission of the fraudulent summons, that the Appellant has failed to provide sufficient reliable evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that he was a genuine Christian Shouter in China and the events did not occur as alleged.
Furthermore, based on the above I find it is unnecessary to deal with the other arguments within the memorandum related to credibility. Sur place
I find that the RPD was correct regarding its overall conclusion about whether there was a sur place claim.

The RPD found that any sur place aspect of the claim must fail that were based and predicated on events in China, which it found not credible. The RPD also found that the church letter does not create a sur place aspect to this claim.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by focusing improperly on motivation instead of on the merits of the documentation provided to conclude that his faith was inauthentic. He also argues that it was an error to determine that his activities in China were relevant to sur place and the focus should have been whether his activities in Canada put him at risk if he returned to China. He submits that these Canadian activities cannot be ignored even if motivation is a concern. He also submits that even if it was correct to find that he converted simply to bolster the claim, good faith is not required for a sur place claim and there is an obligation to consider these activities.

He argues that relying on previous credibility findings is an error because whether he was credible regarding his practice in China, this does not mean that he is not credible or genuine in his Canadian practice. He further argues that the authorities having prior knowledge of his activities in Canada is not a requirement for sur place and must ask not whether there is evidence that this came to the attention of authorities, but rather if on a balance of probabilities, these activities would place him at risk upon return.

I have considered the issue as part of my independent assessment in acknowledgement that even if the Appellant was not a genuine Shouter Christian in China, he could still be at risk if his Shouter activities in Canada came to the attention of the Chinese authorities upon return to China.

Firstly, I have reviewed the documents in question and I find that the RPD was correct in giving them no weight. The RPD found that the Appellant's letter of support from a pastor in Canada did not redeem his lack of credibility and no particular finding was made regarding the photographs.

The letter11 in evidence is from a person named XXXX XXXX, an elder at the Church in Toronto. He indicates that the Appellant has attended Sunday meetings since XXXX XXXX, 2017, he has completed a course and is now eligible for Baptism. While the letter may validate that the Appellant is associated with the Church in Toronto, it does not establish that his practice was indicative of a genuine commitment to the Shouters. I place no evidentiary weight on this document as support for the Appellant's identity as a genuine Christian Shouter and find it does not overcome the significant credibility concerns outlined above.

There are also a number of photographs12 in evidence. I find that although I do not have the originals to examine, these photos are not determinative as they also do not show the genuineness of his practice.

In my review of the record I find that there was no persuasive evidence submitted/adduced at the RPD hearing or in his Basis of Claim (BOC) form to suggest that the Appellant's practice at the Church in Toronto has come to the attention of Chinese authorities, or that he would be perceived to be a genuine Christian of the Shouter denomination upon return to China. He did not provide any evidence to indicate that he, or the group in Toronto, were ever observed, photographed, or approached by or faced harassment from anyone while engaged in Shouter activities. Hence, I find on a balance of probabilities, these activities would not place him at risk upon return.

In this respect, I am guided by the Federal Court Trial Division decision in Wang,13 which held that a sur place claim could not be maintained in the absence of evidence, that the making of the refugee claim had specifically come to the attention of the authorities of the claimant's country of origin.

The Appellant's allegations were that his desire to commence the practice of Christianity took place as a result of circumstances, which occurred in China. He alleges that his practice in Canada is a continuation of the practice he began in China. However, having found that he was not a genuine Shouter in China, I find that his connection to the Church in Toronto in Canada is questionable. Further, having insufficient reliable and persuasive probative evidence of conversion in Canada, I find, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant was not a Shouter in China, nor is he a Shouter in Canada. In the context of the findings noted above, I find that the Appellant affiliated himself with the practice for the sole purpose of supporting and bolstering his claim and he will on a balance of probabilities, not practice on return.

Having reviewed all the evidence in this appeal, I agree with the RPD, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant is not a genuine Christian. I further agree with the RPD, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant is not wanted by the authorities in China because of Shouter Christian activities or for any other reason. I find that the Appellant would not face a serious possibility of persecution, nor would he face a danger of torture or a risk to his life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to China. I confirm the decision of the RPD and dismiss the appeal. (signed) "T. Andrews" T. Andrews March 13, 2020 Date 1 Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v.
